passages.text: So, on the following day in Tyre, I went to the quiet place as we had arranged. After seeing and greeting the others, together with some additional people, but not seeing Appion, I asked why he was not present. Someone said that he had been physically unwell since that very evening. When I said that it was reasonable for us to set out immediately and visit him, almost everyone requested that I first hold a discussion with them and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well. Once everyone had come to a single decision, I began to speak:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσαρρώστως αὐτὸν ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἑσπέρας ἐσχηκέναι τὸ σωμάτιον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he had been physically unwell since that very evening
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom describes the poor condition of his body. The diminutive σωμάτιον need not imply literal smallness and is represented naturally by “physically,” while “that very evening” preserves the intensive force of αὐτῆς.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that I first hold a discussion with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαλέγομαι can mean converse, discourse, or debate; “hold a discussion” suits the requested address without predetermining its degree of formality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἶθ’ οὕτως κἀκεῖνον ἐπισκέψασθαι δύνασθαι αὐτόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, referring to Clement from the participants’ perspective. English naturally returns that third-person reference to the narrator’s first person.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Once everyone had come to a single decision
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, “when one opinion of all had come about”; the rendering expresses their resulting unanimity.

source_issues.issue: The main rendering analyzes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, contextually referring to Clement with a shift from the preceding first-person με to the participants’ third-person perspective. Alternatively, κἀκεῖνον and αὐτόν may be understood as an emphatic or resumptive double reference to Appion, yielding the sense “visit that man himself.” The construction is unusual but does not require deleting either accusative.
